A character that is expressed within the project area as well as the surrounding stream valleys, could be that of wilderness. Wilderness in this case is suggested by the combination of: (1) moderate to steep slopes (up to 125 percent is some areas); (2) dense, almost tropical-like surroundings (Figure 2-31); and (3) turbulance of the streams, which are perceived through visual confrontation, ambient sound level, and high velocities. This combination might provide a sense of being somewhere wild and remote because of the confined, dense, and active spaces involved.
2.5.2 Historical and Archeological Aspects
The National Register of Historic Places and its most recent supplement, dated September 6, 1976, list no historic sites in the vicinity of the proposed Bad Creek Project. The State Historic Preservation Officer has stated that no historic sites or sites eligible for inclusion in the Register are in the area of the proposed project. Keowee Old Town, an important archeological site at the end of Road S-200 on Keowee Lake, is about one-half mile east of the present transmission line and would not be affected by the additional transmission line (Lee, 1974).
In October 1973, John D. Combes of the Institute of Archeology and Anthropology, University of South Carolina, surveyed the proposed project site for archeological remains. None were found, a fact that Dr. Combes attributed to the rugged and difficult nature of the terrain that makes the area unsuitable for human habitation. The survey did not include the route of the proposed transmission line (Combes, 1973).
